meaning: Talking quickly and continuously in a silly or confusing way; also the soft sound of flowing water
trick: BAB-BAB-BAB — a baby making the same sounds again and again.
examples: The baby was babbling happily in her cot.
We sat by the babbling stream.

usage.pattern: someone is babbling (on) about something; a babbling brook/stream

meaning: Said in a way that seems nice but is actually an insult (of a compliment); also a tennis shot hit with the back of the hand facing forward
trick: A BACK-HANDED slap hidden inside a compliment — it looks friendly from the front.
examples: "You look good for your age" is a backhanded compliment.
She hit a strong backhanded shot to win the point.

meaning: Rescued someone from trouble, usually by giving money; also (informal) left or gave up on a plan suddenly
trick: Throwing water OUT of a boat with a BAIL (bucket) to save it.
examples: The government bailed out the failing bank.
He said he'd come to the party, but he bailed out at the last minute.

usage.pattern: bail someone/something out (of something); bail out on someone/something

meaning: Extremely cruel and violent; also wild and uncivilised
trick: BARBARians were wild tribes — anything they'd do is BARBARIC.
examples: Hurting animals for fun is barbaric.
The old punishment was barbaric.

meaning: Sharp, hurtful remarks; also the sharp backward-pointing points on a hook or wire
trick: BARBed wire has sharp points — BARBS are sharp words that stick in you.
examples: She ignored the barbs from her classmates.
The fish hook has small barbs so the fish can't slip off.

usage.pattern: barbs at/about someone; trade barbs (with someone)

meaning: Uncovered or showed something that was hidden (past of bare)
trick: BARE = uncovered; BARED = made it bare.
examples: The dog bared its teeth at the stranger.
She finally bared her feelings to her friend.

meaning: A large farm building for keeping animals, crops or tools
trick: BARN sounds like BORN — calves are often BORN in a BARN.
examples: The cows sleep in the barn at night.
We stored the hay in the barn.

usage.pattern: in the barn / a barn for something

meaning: The area around a farm barn where animals are kept
trick: BARN + YARD — the yard outside the barn.
examples: Chickens were running around the barnyard.
The kids loved the barnyard animals at the farm.

meaning: A large building or group of buildings where soldiers live
trick: BARRACKS = soldiers packed in like a RACK of beds.
examples: The soldiers went back to the barracks after training.
The old army barracks is now a museum.

usage.pos: noun (plural form, used as singular or plural)

meaning: Moved very fast and forcefully, often without control (past)
trick: Like a BARREL rolling down a hill — fast and unstoppable.
examples: The truck barreled down the highway.
He barreled into the room without knocking.

meaning: Moving very fast and forcefully, often without control
trick: A BARREL rolling downhill — it just keeps BARRELING on.
examples: A car came barreling around the corner.
The kids were barreling down the stairs.

meaning: Shy and easily embarrassed
trick: BASH-FUL: so shy you'd rather hide than face a BASH (party).
examples: The bashful boy hid behind his mother.
She gave a bashful smile when they praised her.

usage.pattern: be/feel bashful (about something) / a bashful + noun

meaning: Lying in warmth or sunlight and enjoying it; also enjoying praise or attention
trick: A cat BASKING in the sun, happy as a lizard on a rock.
examples: The cat was basking in the sun by the window.
She was basking in the praise after her speech.

usage.pattern: bask in something (the sun / glory / attention)

meaning: The lowest, deepest sound in music; a guitar or voice that makes this sound (pronounced like 'base')
trick: Bass is the BASE (bottom) of the music — and it sounds like 'base'.
examples: Turn down the bass, the walls are shaking.
He plays bass guitar in a band.

usage.pattern: play (the) bass; the bass (sound) in something

meaning: People who are swimming or bathing; also (Australian informal) a swimsuit
trick: BATHERS are people taking a BATH in the sea.
examples: The beach was full of bathers on Sunday.
Don't forget to pack your bathers for the trip.

meaning: Completely crazy (rude slang, often 'batshit crazy')
trick: Bats fly around wildly in the dark — total madness.
examples: That plan is batshit crazy.
He went batshit when he saw the bill.

meaning: Damaged or hurt by being hit many times; also (food) covered in batter and fried
trick: BAT-tered — hit again and again with a BAT.
examples: He drove an old battered car.
We ordered battered fish and chips.

usage.pattern: battered + noun; be battered by something

meaning: Slightly crazy or strange (informal, mild)
trick: 'Bats in the belfry' — a head full of bats is a bit batty.
examples: My batty old uncle talks to his plants.
The noise is driving me batty.

usage.pattern: someone is a bit batty; something drives someone batty

meaning: Cried loudly; also shouted loudly (past)
trick: BAWL sounds like a BALL of noise: a baby crying loudly.
examples: The baby bawled all night.
The coach bawled at the players to run faster.

usage.pattern: bawl (your eyes out); bawl at someone; bawl something out

meaning: Howling loudly, like dogs or wolves; also loudly demanding something, like an angry crowd
trick: BAY sounds like the howl of a dog at the moon: 'BAAAY!'
examples: We heard dogs baying in the distance.
The crowd was baying for blood.

usage.pattern: be baying (at something); be baying for something

meaning: A huge, uncountable number (informal, made-up number)
trick: Bigger than a billion — a BAZILLION!
examples: I have a bazillion things to do today.
She has asked me that question a bazillion times.

usage.pattern: a bazillion things/times; bazillions of something

meaning: Small balls of glass, wood or plastic with a hole for a string; also small drops of liquid
trick: BEADS on a necklace look like little drops of sweat on your head.
examples: She made a necklace from colourful beads.
Beads of sweat ran down his face.

usage.pattern: beads of something (sweat / water); a string of beads

meaning: A line of light; a long, strong piece of wood or metal holding up a roof; also to smile widely
trick: A torch BEAM, and a face that BEAMS as bright as one.
examples: A beam of sunlight came through the window.
The kids beam with joy when they see their grandma.

usage.pattern: a beam of something; beam at someone / beam with pride

meaning: Smiled very widely and happily; also sent out light (past)
trick: A BEAM of light — her face BEAMED like a torch.
examples: She beamed when she saw her exam results.
The sun beamed through the window.

usage.pattern: beam at someone / beam with pride/joy

meaning: People who carry something, like a coffin, a flag or a message
trick: BEAR = carry. BEARERS carry things.
examples: Six bearers carried the coffin into the church.
The flag bearers led the parade.

meaning: Signalling someone to come closer, usually with a hand; looking inviting
trick: BECKON ≈ 'back on' — waving your hand to say 'come back here'.
examples: The teacher was beckoning me to come to her desk.
The cool water looked beckoning on a hot day.

usage.pattern: beckon (to) someone to do something; beckon someone over

meaning: Too ill or weak to get out of bed
trick: BED + RIDDEN — 'ridden' (stuck) to the bed.
examples: Grandpa was bedridden for a week with the flu.
After the accident, she was bedridden for months.

usage.pattern: be/become bedridden (with an illness / for a time)

meaning: The frame of a bed, without the mattress
trick: BED + STEAD (place): the frame that holds the bed in place.
examples: The old iron bedstead creaked when he sat down.
They painted the wooden bedstead white.

meaning: The state of being confused and unable to think clearly
trick: BE-FUDDLE-ment: your brain is a FUDDLED muddle.
examples: He stared at the maths problem in befuddlement.
To my befuddlement, the shop was closed on a Monday.

meaning: Became the father of (old-fashioned past of 'beget'); also caused or produced something
trick: BEGAT = BEGOT: the old Bible way to say 'had a child'.
examples: Abraham begat Isaac, says the Bible.
One small lie begat many more.

usage.pattern: someone begat someone; something begat something

meaning: A pale, light brown colour, like sand
trick: BEIGE rhymes with 'page' — the colour of an old paper page.
examples: She bought a beige sofa for the living room.
The walls were painted a plain beige.

usage.pattern: a beige something; something is beige; painted beige

meaning: Coming or happening late
trick: BE-LATE-d — it's LATE.
examples: Happy belated birthday!
He sent a belated thank-you note.

meaning: To make someone or something seem small or unimportant
trick: BE-LITTLE — make someone feel LITTLE.
examples: Don't belittle your sister's ideas.
He always tries to belittle other people's work.

meaning: A graph shaped like a bell, showing that most results are in the middle and few are very high or very low
trick: Draw it and it looks like a BELL — tall in the middle, low at the ends.
examples: Most students' marks fell in the middle of the bell curve.
Heights of people follow a bell curve.

usage.pattern: follow a bell curve; on/in the bell curve; grade on a bell curve

meaning: Helpful, useful or good for you
trick: BENE = good (like 'benefit') — something that does you good.
examples: Exercise is beneficial for your health.
The extra class was beneficial to everyone.

meaning: Advantages or good results from something; also money or help given by a company or government
trick: BENE = good + FIT — things that fit in well and do good.
examples: One of the benefits of walking is better sleep.
The job comes with health benefits.

usage.pattern: the benefits of something/doing; something benefits someone; benefit from something

meaning: Kind, generous and wanting to help others
trick: BENE = good (like BENEfit) + VOLENT = wishing. Wishing good things for others.
examples: Our benevolent neighbour helps everyone on the street.
The benevolent king gave food to the poor.

usage.pattern: be benevolent (towards someone) / a benevolent + noun

meaning: Gentle and kind; (of an illness or lump) not harmful or dangerous
trick: BENIGN ≈ 'be nice' — harmless and gentle. Opposite: malignant.
examples: The doctor said the lump was benign.
He gave a benign smile to the children.

usage.pattern: something is benign; a benign tumour/smile

meaning: To scold someone angrily
trick: BE-RATE — RATE someone very badly, loudly.
examples: The coach berated the players for being late.
She berated herself for forgetting the keys.

usage.pattern: berate someone (for something / for doing something)

meaning: A raised bank of earth, such as along a road, canal or trail
trick: BERM sounds like a BUMP of earth by the road.
examples: The car stopped on the grassy berm.
Bikers love jumping over the berms on the trail.

meaning: To give something, especially an honour or gift
trick: BEST-OW — give someone your BEST.
examples: The king will bestow a medal on the hero.
She likes to bestow gifts on her friends.

meaning: Gave something as an honour, gift or reward
trick: BE-STOWED — the king STOWED (placed) a gift in your hands.
examples: The award was bestowed on the best student.
The king bestowed a medal on the brave soldier.

meaning: Was disloyal to someone who trusted you; also showed a feeling you were trying to hide (past)
trick: BE-TRAY-ed: like serving your friend on a TRAY to the enemy.
examples: He felt betrayed when his friend told his secret.
Her shaking voice betrayed her fear.

meaning: Very confused and unable to understand what is happening
trick: BE-WILD-ered — lost in the wild, not knowing which way to go.
examples: He looked bewildered by the long question.
The tourists were bewildered in the busy station.

usage.pattern: be bewildered by/at something; look bewildered

meaning: Related to the Bible; also (informal) very large or extreme
trick: BIBLE + -ical — and the Bible has huge floods.
examples: The town was hit by a flood of biblical proportions.
She knows many biblical stories.

meaning: Riding a bicycle
trick: BI-CYCLE-ing — riding on two (BI) wheels.
examples: We went bicycling in the park on Sunday.
Bicycling to work keeps him fit.

meaning: A stand on which a coffin or dead body is placed before burial
trick: BIER sounds like BEER, but it's a sad stand for a coffin, not a drink.
examples: The coffin rested on a bier in the hall.
They carried the bier slowly to the grave.

meaning: Fairly big
trick: BIG + -ish = sort of big.
examples: They live in a biggish house near the park.
He's a biggish man with a loud voice.

meaning: Unfair dislike of people because of their religion, race or beliefs
trick: A BIG-OT has a BIG head and a small mind.
examples: We must speak out against bigotry.
Her speech was full of bigotry.

meaning: An important or powerful person (informal)
trick: In the old days, important men wore BIG WIGs.
examples: Some company bigwigs visited our office.
He acts like a bigwig, but he's just a clerk.

usage.pattern: a bigwig in/at something (a company, politics)

meaning: A bitter liquid made by the liver; also bitter anger
trick: BILE is bitter — like a BITTER BILL you hate to pay.
examples: The patient vomited bile.
His words were full of bile.

meaning: Feeling sick in the stomach; also bad-tempered; also a nasty, sickly colour
trick: BILE + -ious: too much BILE makes you sick and grumpy.
examples: The boat ride left me feeling bilious.
He painted the room a bilious green.

meaning: A game played on a cloth-covered table with balls and a long stick called a cue
trick: BILLIARDS: hit the BALLS with a cue, a cousin of pool and snooker.
examples: Grandpa loves playing billiards at the club.
They have a billiards table in the basement.

usage.pattern: play billiards / a game of billiards

meaning: Swelled out or rose in large waves or clouds (past)
trick: A PILLOW puffing up — the smoke BILLOWED.
examples: Smoke billowed from the chimney.
Her dress billowed in the wind.

meaning: Swelling out or rising in large waves or clouds
trick: Puffy like a PILLOW — BILLOWING clouds.
examples: Billowing smoke filled the sky.
The sails were billowing in the breeze.

usage.pattern: billowing + noun; be billowing in/from something

meaning: Folders with rings or clips for holding loose papers together
trick: They BIND your papers together.
examples: Keep your notes in these binders.
She has three binders full of recipes.

meaning: Containers for rubbish or for storing things
trick: BINS hold the stuff you put IN them.
examples: Please take the bins out tonight.
We keep rice in big plastic bins.

usage.pattern: put something in the bins; take the bins out

meaning: A tree with thin, smooth, white or silver bark
trick: BIRCH: a white tree where BIRDS perch.
examples: A tall birch tree grows in our garden.
The birch bark peeled off like paper.

meaning: Very strange or unusual
trick: BIZARRE sounds like 'bazaar' — a crowded market full of strange things.
examples: I had a bizarre dream last night.
It was bizarre to see snow in summer.

usage.pattern: something is bizarre; it is bizarre that ...

meaning: Times when the electricity goes off; also moments of losing consciousness or memory
trick: Everything goes BLACK — the lights are OUT.
examples: We had three blackouts during the storm.
He suffers from blackouts after drinking.

meaning: Without much taste, interest or excitement
trick: BLAND rhymes with SAND — no flavour at all.
examples: The soup was bland, so I added salt.
The movie was a bit bland.

meaning: Made a very loud, harsh sound (past)
trick: BLARE sounds like a BLAST of noise.
examples: Music blared from the car.
The horn blared behind us.

meaning: Making a very loud, harsh sound
trick: BLARING = BLASTING noise.
examples: The TV was blaring in the next room.
He drove past with music blaring.

usage.pattern: with something blaring; a blaring + noun

meaning: Done openly and obviously, without any shame (usually something bad)
trick: BLATANT ≈ 'blast it out' — done loudly, for everyone to see.
examples: That was a blatant lie.
He made a blatant mistake in front of everyone.

meaning: A large, strong fire; or a very bright light
trick: BLAZE ≈ 'blast of flames'.
examples: Firefighters put out the blaze quickly.
The garden was a blaze of colour in spring.

usage.pattern: a blaze (fire); something blazes; a blaze of colour/light

meaning: Burning brightly and strongly; also very hot, or very fast
trick: A BLAZE is a big fire — BLAZING is burning like one.
examples: We sat around the blazing fire.
It was a blazing hot day.

usage.pattern: blazing + noun / blazing hot / with guns blazing

meaning: Cold, empty and unwelcoming; also without hope
trick: BLEAK sounds like BLACK + WEAK — dark and hopeless.
examples: The future looked bleak after he lost his job.
It was a bleak, grey winter morning.

meaning: Made the 'baa' sound of a sheep or goat; also complained in a weak, whiny way (past)
trick: BLEAT sounds like the sheep's 'BLEEEH'.
examples: The lamb bleated for its mother.
He bleated about how unfair the test was.

meaning: Making the 'baa' sound of a sheep or goat; also complaining in a weak, whiny way
trick: BLEEEH-ting: the sound a goat makes.
examples: We could hear goats bleating in the field.
Stop bleating about the weather!

meaning: Lost blood (past of bleed)
trick: BLEED → BLED, like FEED → FED.
examples: His knee bled after he fell.
The colour bled when I washed the shirt.

meaning: So bright or strong that you cannot see properly
trick: It makes you BLIND for a moment.
examples: The sun was blinding when we came out.
There was a blinding flash of light.

usage.pattern: a blinding light/flash; something is blinding

meaning: Window coverings that can be pulled down or turned to block light
trick: They make the window BLIND — no light gets in.
examples: Please close the blinds, the sun is too bright.
She opened the blinds to let the light in.

meaning: Perfect happiness
trick: BLISS sounds like a sweet KISS — pure happiness.
examples: Lying on the beach was pure bliss.
Ignorance is bliss.

meaning: A small bubble on the skin filled with liquid, caused by rubbing or burning
trick: New shoes make a BLISTER — a little BUBBLE on your skin.
examples: My new shoes gave me a blister.
Don't pop the blister on your hand.

meaning: Very hot; very fast; or very angry and harsh
trick: So hot it gives you BLISTERS.
examples: We walked in the blistering heat.
The runner set a blistering pace.

meaning: Small bubbles on the skin filled with liquid, caused by rubbing or burning
trick: One BLISTER, two BLISTERS — bubbles on your skin.
examples: After the long walk, I had blisters on my feet.
Holding the bat all day gave him blisters.

meaning: In a happy, carefree way, often without thinking about problems
trick: BLITHE sounds like BLISS: carefree and happy, maybe too carefree.
examples: She blithely ignored the warning signs.
He walked blithely into the rain without an umbrella.

meaning: Attacked quickly and strongly; also (informal slang) very drunk
trick: The BLITZ was a fast bombing attack — BLITZED = hit hard (or hit hard by drinks).
examples: The team blitzed their opponents in the first half.
He got blitzed at the party last night.

meaning: Swollen and too full, often from eating too much or from gas
trick: Like a BOAT puffed up with air — BLOATED.
examples: I felt bloated after the big lunch.
The company has a bloated budget.

usage.pattern: feel bloated (after something); a bloated budget/system

meaning: Small round drops or lumps of a thick liquid or soft substance
trick: BLOB sounds like a soft PLOP: a messy drop.
examples: There were blobs of paint on the floor.
He dropped blobs of cream on the cake.

meaning: Producing flowers; growing healthily; also (British informal) used for emphasis, like 'bloody'
trick: A BLOOM is a flower — BLOOMING = flowers opening.
examples: The roses are blooming in the garden.
That blooming dog woke me up again!

meaning: Produced flowers; or grew and developed in a good way
trick: BLOSSOM = flower — something that bloomed like a flower.
examples: The cherry trees blossomed in April.
She blossomed into a confident speaker.

usage.pattern: something blossomed; someone blossomed into something

meaning: Irregular patches or marks of colour, often on the skin
trick: BLOTCH = BLOT + SPLOTCH: messy patches.
examples: She had red blotches on her face from the heat.
The old wall was covered in damp blotches.

meaning: Moving air, as the wind does; also sending out air from your mouth
trick: BLOW → BLOWING: what the wind keeps doing.
examples: The wind is blowing hard today.
She was blowing out the candles on her cake.

meaning: A big party or celebration; an easy, one-sided win; or a sudden burst tyre
trick: Everything BLOWS OUT — a huge party, a huge win, or a tyre that bursts.
examples: They had a blowout party for her birthday.
Our team won the match in a blowout, 6–0.

usage.pattern: have a blowout (party); win in a blowout; a tyre blowout

meaning: Not sharp; also saying what you think very directly
trick: A BLUNT knife can't cut — a BLUNT person doesn't soften words.
examples: This knife is too blunt to cut bread.
To be blunt, your idea won't work.

usage.pattern: be blunt (with someone) / to be blunt,

meaning: Loud, aggressive or proud talk with little effect; (of wind) to blow in strong gusts
trick: BLUSTER ≈ 'blow + bluff' — lots of wind and noise, nothing real.
examples: Ignore his bluster; he won't really do anything.
The wind blustered all night.

usage.pattern: someone's bluster; someone blusters (about something); the wind blusters

meaning: A wild pig; also a male pig
trick: A BOAR is never BORING: a wild, tusked pig.
examples: A wild boar ran across the forest path.
The farmer keeps one boar and ten sows.

meaning: A very large amount (informal)
trick: Enough to fill a whole BOAT.
examples: He made a boatload of money.
We have a boatload of homework this week.

meaning: To move up and down quickly, especially on water; also a short hairstyle
trick: A fishing BOB goes up and down on the water.
examples: The boat bobbed on the waves.
She cut her hair into a bob.

usage.pattern: bob up and down / bob your head

meaning: Moving up and down quickly, especially on water
trick: BOB-BOB-BOBBING — a duck going up and down.
examples: Ducks were bobbing on the lake.
He was bobbing his head to the music.

usage.pattern: be bobbing (up and down) on something

meaning: Imaginary things that scare people; also bits of dried mucus from the nose (informal); in golf, one shot over par
trick: BOGEYman — scary things in the dark.
examples: Stop picking your bogeys!
He made two bogeys on the last holes.

meaning: Fake, false or not genuine
trick: BOGUS ≈ 'bogey' — a scary fake thing that isn't real.
examples: The email was a bogus offer.
He showed a bogus ID card.

usage.pattern: a bogus something; something is bogus

meaning: To support or strengthen something; also a long pillow
trick: A BOLSTER pillow holds you UP — so to BOLSTER is to support.
examples: The good news bolstered her confidence.
The company hired more staff to bolster sales.

meaning: To run away suddenly; also a metal pin used to lock a door or join things; a flash of lightning
trick: Usain BOLT — he runs off super fast.
examples: The horse bolted when it heard the noise.
Lock the door with the bolt.

usage.pattern: bolt (from/out of somewhere); a bolt of lightning

meaning: Attacked continuously; or given too many questions, messages or things at once
trick: Like being hit by BOMBs again and again.
examples: The singer was bombarded with questions.
My phone was bombarded with messages.

usage.pattern: be bombarded with something; bombard someone with something

meaning: The state of being a slave or not free; also tying someone up for sexual pleasure
trick: BOND-age — being held in BONDS (chains).
examples: The slaves were finally freed from bondage.
He felt his job was a kind of bondage.

meaning: A large outdoor fire, often for celebration or burning rubbish
trick: BON-FIRE — a good (BON) FIRE for a party.
examples: We roasted marshmallows on the bonfire.
They lit a bonfire on the beach.

meaning: Hitting lightly on the head (informal); also having sex (rude slang)
trick: BONK — the sound of a soft hit on the head.
examples: He kept bonking his brother with a pillow.
The ball came bonking off his head.

meaning: Made a deep, loud sound; also grew quickly and became successful (past)
trick: BOOM! A big loud sound, or business going BOOM.
examples: Thunder boomed across the sky.
Online shopping boomed during the lockdown.

meaning: Came back to hurt the person who started it (past)
trick: A BOOMERANG comes back to you — and so did the plan.
examples: His lie boomeranged on him.
The plan boomeranged and caused more trouble.

meaning: Making a deep, loud sound; also growing very fast and successful
trick: BOOM! — loud — and business going BOOM upward.
examples: He spoke in a booming voice.
The tech industry is booming.

usage.pattern: a booming + noun; something is booming

meaning: Very close to a limit; only just acceptable or not
trick: Standing right on the BORDER LINE — not clearly on either side.
examples: His marks were borderline for passing.

meaning: A wide city street, often lined with trees

examples: We walked down the tree-lined boulevard.
The café is on the main boulevard.

meaning: Running or jumping with big, energetic leaps
trick: BOUNDING like a kangaroo: it jumps past the BOUNDary.
examples: The puppy came bounding towards me.
She went bounding up the stairs.

meaning: A short period of illness or activity; also a boxing or wrestling match
trick: A BOUT of flu is ABOUT a few days.
examples: She had a bout of flu last week.
The boxing bout lasted ten rounds.

meaning: To bend your head or body forward to show respect (rhymes with 'cow'); also a knot with two loops, or a curved weapon for shooting arrows (rhymes with 'go')
trick: Two sounds: BOW (cow) to the king; tie a BOW (go) on a gift.
examples: The actors bow at the end of the show.
She tied a red bow on the present.

usage.pattern: bow to someone / bow your head; tie a bow

meaning: A window that curves outward from the wall of a building
trick: Shaped like a BOW (the curved weapon), bending out of the wall.
examples: They had a big bow window in the front room.
The cat sat in the bow window watching the street.

usage.pattern: a (big) bow window; in the bow window

meaning: A simple knot that makes a fixed loop at the end of a rope
trick: BOW + LINE — a loop tied in the line at the BOW of a ship.
examples: The sailor tied a bowline around the post.
Learning the bowline is the first lesson in sailing.

meaning: Twisted three or more strands of hair or rope together (past); also having braids
trick: BRAID = plait — BRAIDED hair is plaited hair.

He wore a braided leather bracelet.

meaning: (Slang, joking) Ideas or facts so interesting they excite your mind

examples: Space facts give me brain boners.

meaning: Waving something, especially a weapon, in a threatening or excited way
trick: BRAND-ishing: waving a burning BRAND (torch) at someone.
examples: The robber ran in brandishing a knife.
Fans were brandishing flags in the stadium.

usage.pattern: be brandishing something (a weapon / a flag)

meaning: Too confident and loud in a rude way
trick: BRASH sounds like RASH — acting without thinking.
examples: The brash young player annoyed his teammates.
His brash comments upset everyone.

meaning: Breaking a rule, law or promise; or a gap or break in a wall or defence
trick: BREACH ≈ BREAK — both start with BRE.
examples: Sharing the password was a breach of the rules.
Water came through a breach in the wall.

usage.pattern: a breach of something (rules/contract/trust); breach a rule/wall

meaning: Raised animals or plants to produce young ones (past of 'breed'); also, brought up
trick: BRED = past of BREED — 'born and bred'.
examples: He was born and bred in Mumbai.
These dogs were bred to guard sheep.

usage.pattern: be bred for/to do something; born and bred (in a place)

meaning: Short trousers that stop just below the knee, worn for horse riding or in old times
trick: BREECHES sound like BRITCHES: old-style riding pants.
examples: The rider wore white breeches and tall boots.
In old paintings, men wear breeches and stockings.

meaning: Keeping animals or plants to produce young ones; also good manners learned from your family
trick: BREED → BREEDING: making more of the same BREED.
examples: Spring is the breeding season for many birds.
They are breeding dogs on their farm.

meaning: Types of animals within a species; or produces young ones or causes something
trick: Dog BREEDS — Labrador, Pug, Beagle.
examples: There are many breeds of dogs.
Laziness breeds more laziness.

usage.pattern: breeds of something; something breeds something (causes it)

meaning: Did something very easily; also walked in a casual, confident way (past)
trick: Easy like a BREEZE.
examples: She breezed through the exam.
He breezed into the room, smiling.

usage.pattern: breeze through something; breeze in/into somewhere

meaning: Doing something very easily; also moving casually and confidently
trick: A BREEZE flows easily — BREEZING through.
examples: He is breezing through his homework.
She came breezing in late as usual.

usage.pattern: be breezing through something; come breezing in

meaning: (informal) Made an electronic device completely useless, like a brick; also built or blocked with bricks (past)
trick: Your phone is now just a BRICK.
examples: The update bricked my phone.
They bricked up the old window.

usage.pattern: brick something (a device); brick something up

meaning: The top edge of a cup or bowl; also the flat edge sticking out around a hat
trick: BRIM: filled to the very RIM.
examples: She filled the glass to the brim.
He wore a hat with a wide brim.

usage.pattern: fill something to the brim; brim with something

meaning: Very salty water, used for pickling food; also seawater
trick: BRINE: BRING the salt.
examples: The olives are kept in brine.
Soak the chicken in brine before cooking.

usage.pattern: in brine / soak something in brine

meaning: The edge of a steep place; the point just before something happens ('on the brink of')
trick: BRINK ≈ BRIM — right at the edge, about to spill over.
examples: The company was on the brink of closing.
She stood at the brink of the cliff.

usage.pattern: be on the brink of something / of doing something

meaning: Quickly and with energy
trick: BRISK = QUICK; BRISKLY = quickly and actively.
examples: We walked briskly to keep warm.
She spoke briskly and got to the point.

meaning: A family of young birds hatched together; also to keep thinking unhappily about something
trick: A hen sits on her BROOD; a sad person sits and BROODS over a problem.
examples: The hen sat on her brood of chicks.
Don't brood over one bad grade.

usage.pattern: a brood of something; brood over/about something

meaning: The forehead; also an eyebrow; the top of a hill
trick: BROW is the top of your face — EYEBROW sits on it.
examples: He wiped the sweat from his brow.
The car stopped at the brow of the hill.

usage.pattern: wipe your brow; furrow your brow; the brow of a hill

meaning: Small, square chocolate cakes; also young girls in the junior Girl Guides
trick: BROWN + ies — little BROWN chocolate squares.
examples: Mom baked brownies for the party.
These chocolate brownies are so soft.

meaning: Having a dark mark on the skin from being hit; also emotionally hurt
trick: BRUISE — the blue-purple mark after a bump.
examples: He bruised his knee when he fell.
She felt bruised after the argument.

meaning: A woman or girl with dark brown hair
trick: BRUN = brown (French) — BRUNETTE has brown hair.
examples: The brunette in the red dress is my cousin.
She dyed her hair from blonde to brunette.

meaning: The main force or worst part of something bad ('bear the brunt of')
trick: BRUNT ≈ 'brunt = blunt hit' — you take the hardest hit.
examples: The coastal towns bore the brunt of the storm.
I took the brunt of the blame.

meaning: Annoying or bothering someone again and again (informal)
trick: Like a BUG buzzing around your head — it keeps bugging you.
examples: Stop bugging me while I'm working!
Something has been bugging me all day.

usage.pattern: something is bugging someone; stop bugging someone (about something)

meaning: Round and fat, like a bulb
trick: Shaped like a light BULB: round and swollen.
examples: The clown had a red, bulbous nose.
A bulbous vase sat on the table.

meaning: A round lump that sticks out; also to swell out
trick: A BULGE is a BUMP that sticks out.
examples: There was a bulge in his pocket.
Her bag was so full it started to bulge.

usage.pattern: a bulge in something; bulge with something

meaning: Swelled out in a round shape (past)
trick: A BULGE is a lump sticking out — BULGED = stuck out.
examples: His pockets bulged with sweets.
Her eyes bulged in surprise.

meaning: Swelling out in a round shape; very full
trick: BULGING bag — about to burst.
examples: He carried a bulging bag of shopping.
The bodybuilder had bulging muscles.

usage.pattern: bulging + noun / be bulging with something

meaning: (Informal) A homeless or lazy person; the buttocks (British); 'bummed' means sad
trick: A BUM just sits on his BUM all day.
examples: Don't be a lazy bum, get up and help!
He fell on his bum on the ice.

usage.pattern: a lazy bum; on your bum; bum something off someone (borrow)

meaning: Met someone by chance; also hit something by accident (past)
trick: You BUMP INTO a friend like you BUMP INTO a door: without planning it.
examples: I bumped into my old teacher at the mall.
He bumped into the table and spilled his tea.

meaning: The ability to float in water or air; also cheerfulness
trick: A BUOY floats — BUOYANCY is floating power.
examples: Salt water gives you more buoyancy.
Her buoyancy kept the team cheerful.

meaning: Able to float; also cheerful and confident
trick: BUOY + ANT — even an ant floats like a BUOY.
examples: Wood is buoyant, so it floats.
She was in a buoyant mood after the win.

meaning: Floating objects in water that mark safe paths or warn of danger
trick: BOYS floating in the sea — BUOYS.
examples: Red buoys marked the swimming area.
The boat was tied to one of the buoys.

meaning: The act of putting a dead body in the ground
trick: BURY → BURIAL: the act of BURYing.
examples: The burial took place on Sunday morning.
The family chose a quiet burial.

usage.pattern: the burial of someone / a burial + noun

meaning: Put into the ground and covered; also hidden under something (past of bury)
trick: BURY → BURIED, like CARRY → CARRIED.
examples: The dog buried its bone in the garden.
My keys were buried under a pile of clothes.

usage.pattern: bury something; be buried in/under something

meaning: Mexican food: a soft flour tortilla rolled around a filling like beans, rice and meat
trick: BURRITO = 'little donkey' in Spanish — it carries all the filling.
examples: We had burritos for dinner.
She ordered two chicken burritos.

meaning: A hole or tunnel dug by an animal to live in; also to dig or snuggle into something
trick: A rabbit BURROWS a tunnel to hide from the BURRow-er (borrower).
examples: The rabbit hid in its burrow.
The child burrowed under the blankets.

meaning: To suddenly start doing something, such as laughing or crying; also to rush out of somewhere
trick: Like a balloon that BURSTS: the laugh comes OUT suddenly.
examples: She burst out laughing at the joke.
The kids burst out of the classroom when the bell rang.

usage.pattern: burst out doing something (laughing / crying); burst out of somewhere

meaning: Breaking open suddenly; also very full, or very eager to do something
trick: So full it's BURSTING, like an overfilled balloon.
examples: My bag is bursting with books.
She was bursting to tell us the news.

usage.pattern: be bursting with something; be bursting to do something

meaning: A unit for measuring dry goods like grain or fruit (about 35 litres); also (informal) a large amount
trick: A BUSH full of apples fills one BUSHEL basket.
examples: We picked a bushel of apples at the farm.
She has a bushel of ideas for the party.

meaning: Units for measuring dry goods like grain or fruit; also (informal) large amounts
trick: One BUSHEL, many BUSHELS: baskets full of crops.
examples: The farm grows thousands of bushels of corn.
He made bushels of money from his business.

meaning: Attacked by surprise from a hiding place; also cut a path through thick bushes (past)
trick: Someone hiding in the BUSH WHACKED you.
examples: The soldiers were bushwhacked on the jungle road.
We bushwhacked our way through the forest.

usage.pattern: be bushwhacked (by someone); bushwhack through somewhere

meaning: Kept yourself busy with something (past)
trick: BUSY → BUSIED: made yourself BUSY.
examples: She busied herself in the kitchen.
He busied himself with emails to avoid talking.

usage.pattern: busy yourself with something / (in) doing something

meaning: Hit something with the head or horns (past); also pushed into a conversation rudely (butted in)
trick: A goat BUTTED me with its head.
examples: The goat butted the gate with its horns.
He butted in while I was talking.

meaning: A small hole for a button; also to stop someone and make them listen to you
trick: Stop someone by holding their BUTTONHOLE so they can't walk away.
examples: The button won't fit through the buttonhole.
A salesman tried to buttonhole me at the door.

meaning: A low humming sound like a bee; or a feeling of excitement
trick: The sound a bee makes — bzzzz!
examples: I heard the buzz of a bee near the window.
There was a buzz of excitement in the room.

usage.pattern: the buzz of something; a buzz of excitement; something buzzes

meaning: Slowly and gradually, little by little
trick: Like a thermometer rising one DEGREE at a time.
examples: By degrees, the room got warmer.
She got better by degrees after the illness.

usage.pattern: by degrees + sentence / something happens by degrees
